title: Lil Kev Season 2 Trailer Sends Kevin Hart's Young Alter Ego to Juvenile Detention
excerpt:
The animated comedy returns with a more serious predicament for young Kev.
Season 2 premieres on Paramount+ on December 9, 2026.
body_md:
The official trailer for the second season of Lil Kev puts its twelve-year-old protagonist in considerably more trouble than usual. A slow-speed police chase ends with Kev entering juvenile detention, setting up a new chapter of the animated comedy starring Kevin Hart as a fictionalized younger version of himself. Paramount+ has scheduled the season premiere for December 9, 2026.

The series takes place in North Philadelphia in 1993. Young Kev approaches everyday problems with oversized ambitions, relentless imagination and a habit of turning small situations into elaborate schemes. His family supplies much of the show's comic tension: protective mother Nancy, recovering father Henry, cynical older brother Robert and uncle Richard Jr., who has a history of incarceration.

School rivalries, neighborhood schemes and family setbacks have provided the backdrop for Kev's adventures. Season two changes the stakes after an impulsive act of defiance brings him into contact with the juvenile justice system. The official description emphasizes that he is suddenly facing an adult world for which he is not prepared.

Hart returns as the voice of Kev, with Wanda Sykes playing Nancy, Gerald 'Slink' Johnson as Henry, Jamar Malachi Neighbors as Robert and Deon Cole as Richard Jr. Returning performers also include Cree Summer, Loretta Devine, Mo Collins and several other familiar members of the ensemble.

Matthew Claybrooks and Michael Price serve as executive producers and showrunners. Hart is among the executive producers working through Hartbeat, while ShadowMachine leads the animation work. Musa Brooker is the supervising director, and additional executive producers represent both Hartbeat and ShadowMachine.

The new trailer suggests the series will continue balancing exaggerated childhood comedy with the complications of family and community life. However, the brief footage does not establish how long Kev remains in detention or how the storyline resolves, and those details should not be treated as confirmed.

For viewers who followed the first season, the central appeal remains the contrast between Kev's enormous confidence and his limited understanding of the consequences around him. Season two appears ready to test that confidence in a much less forgiving environment while preserving the show's comic voice.
